> **Design rule:** the agent never writes through `\\wsl.localhost`. Every read, write, edit and sea
rch becomes one `wsl.exe -d <distro> -e bash -lc <script>`, so the work happens on the Linux side of
the boundary, as ordinary Linux commands.
## Why
`\\wsl.localhost` is a 9p share, not a Windows filesystem:
- Windows-side writers use "temp file + rename", which that share cannot do — writing from a UNC pat

h fails, and fails deterministically under a read-only sandbox;
- a workspace gets its ACL rewritten
before anything is tagged, but a 9p share returns no security descriptor — `Get-Acl` throws, so a W
indows-side shell cannot start in a `\\wsl.localhost\` workspace at all.
A single Windows-side process also speaks for one distribution at a time: point it at a file in anot
her distro and the path resolves to the first one.
This plugin sidesteps both: it talks to `wsl.exe` directly and executes inside whichever distributio
n the request names, so a WSL workspace, a second distro and a stopped distro are each exactly what
uest names, so a WSL workspace, a second distro and a stopped distro are each exactly what they are.
## How it works
Two halves that meet over the harness web server:
- **Host half** (`index.js`, `lib/*.js`) registers seven routes under `/__wsl_plugin__/` — distro li
sting, directory listing, administration, configuration, runtime status, logs — plus the six `wslx-*

` tools. Requests from anything but the owner web session are rejected.
- **Client half** (`client.j
s`) renders the Settings page and the new-session entry, and calls those routes with the session the
ttings page and the new-session entry, and calls those routes with the session the page already has.
Distribution resolution, in order:
1. the explicit `distro` argument (validated against `wsl -l -q`; a wrong name lists what is install

ed);
2. the distro of the workspace the session runs in (read from `\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\...`);

3. the `DSH_WSL_DISTRO` environment variable (useful with Windows-path workspaces);
4. otherwise `ws
l.exe`'s own default — and every tool prints the distribution it actually ran in, so a fallback is v
isible instead of silent.
Working directories map back the other way: `/home/...` stays as written, `C:\Users\...` becomes `/m
nt/c/Users/...`, and a UNC path maps to its Linux form.
## Settings page
Three tabs under **Settings → WSL**:
| Tab | What it does |
| Distros | Each distribution's state and WSL version, plus start, stop, set default and switching b

etween WSL 1 and 2. |
| Config | `.wslconfig` (global) and `/etc/wsl.conf` (per distro): memory cap,
processor count, swap, networking mode, localhost forwarding, systemd, default user — as a form, wi

th a raw-text view alongside. |
| Runtime | Memory and disk usage, load, uptime, listening ports and
process count for one distribution, from plain Linux tools (`free -b`, `df -B1`, `ss`, `/proc`). |
Deliberate choices:
- **Disk writes happen on save, not on typing.** Each file is written its own way: `.wslconfig` thro
ugh a temp file and an atomic rename, `/etc/wsl.conf` through `wsl.exe -u root`. Comments and unknow

n keys survive.
- **Saving does not restart WSL.** The page says so and offers a restart button; `ws

l --shutdown` asks for confirmation first, because it stops every distribution.
- **Every write keep
s a backup:** `.wslconfig.bak-<date>` and `/etc/wsl.conf.bak-<date>`, and the page shows where it la

nded.
- **Destructive buttons have their own gate.** When the deployment's default permission is not
`danger-full-access`, stopping a distro, switching its version, exporting a disk and `wsl --shutdow
n` all require a confirmation, and the host rejects any request without the matching `acknowledge`.
This is not a sandbox — the model and the page share one authenticated browser session — it guards a

gainst a misclick.
- **A stopped distribution is never started implicitly.** Reading `/etc/wsl.conf`
means running a command inside the distro, which would wake it; a stopped distro therefore shows an
explanation and a start button only. Directory browsing behaves the same way and answers `distro-st

opped`.
- **Dropdowns are drawn by the page.** A native `<select>` popup follows the system palette,
and on a dark theme the highlighted row is unreadable.
## New-session entry
Next to the other entry points on the new-session page there is a **🐧 WSL 目录** button. It opens a di
stro-and-directory picker; "choose this directory" creates a `\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\<path>` works
pace and switches the draft session to it, exactly what the built-in workspace picker does for Windo
es the draft session to it, exactly what the built-in workspace picker does for Windows directories.
## Tools
| Tool | What it does |
| `wslx-run` | Run a bash command inside a distribution (`rg`, `git`, `make`, `python3`…); optional

`workdir` and `timeoutMs`; dangerous commands are intercepted. |
| `wslx-read` | Read a file with li

ne numbers, 2000 lines per call. |
| `wslx-write` | Write a whole file through a Linux-side stdin pi

pe. |
| `wslx-edit` | Replace one exact string; the file's mode and owner stay unchanged. |
| `wslx-

search` | Regex search with `rg`, falling back to `grep -E`; at most 250 matches. |
| `wslx-bg` | Ke
ep a process alive across calls: `start` (a command, or `mode=shell` for an interactive `bash -i`),
`output` (incremental, by cursor), `input` (one line to stdin), `kill`, `list`. |
Every tool accepts `asRoot: true`, which runs that one call as the distribution's Linux root through
`wsl.exe -u root`. The Windows process itself needs no elevation — it uses the root the distro alre
ady has. The names carry a `wslx-` prefix, so they never collide with another bundle's tool names.
## Background tasks and interactive shells
`wslx-bg` keeps one `wsl.exe` child process per task:
- `start` with `mode=command` runs a bash command, and its output stays readable after it finishes;
`mode=shell` keeps an interactive `bash -i`, so `python3 -i`, `psql`, `ssh`, an MQTT client and a `s

udo` password prompt all work a line at a time.
- `output` returns only what was written after the c

ursor you pass, so polling a noisy task does not re-read the log.
